items.stem: Define a testable question.
items.answer: A question that can be answered by doing an experiment or collecting evidence
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A testable question – a question that can be answered by doing an experiment or collecting evidence.

items.stem: Which of the following is a question that cannot be tested in an experiment?
items.answer: Is a rose nicer than a lotus?
items.markingKey: (b) Is a rose nicer than a lotus? is a question that cannot be tested in an experiment. The others: Does a wet cloth dry faster in the sun than in the shade? – a testable question; Does sugar dissolve faster when stirred? – a testable question; Does salt dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water? – a testable question.
options: Does sugar dissolve faster when stirred?
Is a rose nicer than a lotus?
Does salt dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water?
Does a wet cloth dry faster in the sun than in the shade?

items.stem: Which of the following statements is an observation?
items.answer: The thermometer reads 38 °C.
items.markingKey: (d) The thermometer reads 38 °C. is an observation. The others: The child has a fever. – an inference; The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat. – an inference; The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air. – an inference.
options: The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat.
The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air.

items.stem: Kabir sees that the iron gate at his school rusts faster during the monsoon. Frame a testable question and say what he could compare.
items.answer: Question: Does moisture make iron rust faster? Compare two iron nails, one kept in a dry closed bottle and one in moist air, for a week.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable question. 1 mark: a fair comparison.

items.stem:
Read: Meera saw that curd sets quickly in summer but takes much longer in winter. She wondered why. Her grandmother said curd needs warmth.
(i) Write Meera's observation. (ii) Frame a testable question. (iii) Suggest a simple test using two bowls of milk with a spoon of curd each. (iv) What result would support her grandmother's idea?
items.answer: (i) Curd sets faster in summer. (ii) Does temperature affect how fast curd sets? (iii) Keep one bowl in a warm place and one in the refrigerator for 8 hours. (iv) Curd sets in the warm bowl but not (or less) in the cold one.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each part.

items.stem: Two students observe that a puddle dries up faster on a sunny day. One says, "The Sun sucks up the water." How would you turn this into a testable idea and check it?
items.answer: Testable idea: water evaporates faster when it is warmer. Test: keep equal amounts of water in identical plates in sun and shade and measure how long each takes to dry.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable idea. 1 mark: fair comparison. 1 mark: what is measured.

items.stem: Sort these statements into an inference and an observation: (1) The child has a fever; (2) The iron nail has a brown coating; (3) The milk has turned sour and smells bad; (4) The plant has not been watered for days
items.answer: An inference: The child has a fever; The plant has not been watered for days. An observation: The iron nail has a brown coating; The milk has turned sour and smells bad.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): An inference: The child has a fever; The plant has not been watered for days. An observation: The iron nail has a brown coating; The milk has turned sour and smells bad.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A conclusion or explanation we draw from observations, such as guessing that a yellow leaf lacks water."
items.answer: an inference
items.markingKey: (d) An inference is a conclusion or explanation we draw from observations, such as guessing that a yellow leaf lacks water.

items.stem: Which statement about scientific ideas is correct?
items.answer: They can change when new evidence is found
items.markingKey: (c) Scientific knowledge is open to revision with new evidence.
options: They do not need any evidence
They are accepted only if a famous scientist says so
They can change when new evidence is found
They never change once written in a book

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Scientific knowledge can change over time.
Reason (R): New observations and evidence can show that an earlier idea was incomplete or wrong.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) Both true; new evidence is the reason ideas change.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is an inference?
items.answer: The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air.
items.markingKey: (b) The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air. is an inference. The others: The iron nail has a brown coating. – an observation; The thermometer reads 38 °C. – an observation; The candle flame went out when covered with a glass. – an observation.
options: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass.
The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air.
The iron nail has a brown coating.

items.stem: Why should observations be recorded immediately and honestly, even if they are unexpected?
items.answer: Memory is unreliable, and unexpected results are also evidence that may change our idea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: accurate record. 1 mark: unexpected results are useful evidence.

items.stem: Convert this vague question into a testable one: "Why are some fruits better?"
items.answer: For example: "Does a banana kept in the refrigerator stay fresh longer than one kept at room temperature?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: question names what is changed and what is observed/measured.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is an inference?
items.answer: The child has a fever.
items.markingKey: (a) The child has a fever. is an inference. The others: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass. – an observation; The leaves of the plant are drooping. – an observation; The puddle was smaller by evening. – an observation.
options: The leaves of the plant are drooping.
The puddle was smaller by evening.
The candle flame went out when covered with a glass.

items.stem: What is meant by a hypothesis?
items.answer: A possible explanation or answer to a question that can be tested
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A hypothesis – a possible explanation or answer to a question that can be tested.

items.stem: Rohan thinks that plants grow better in sunlight. Which of these is the hypothesis being tested?
items.answer: Plants need sunlight to grow well.
items.markingKey: (a) The hypothesis is the testable idea: "Plants need sunlight to grow well."
options: Plants need sunlight to grow well.
Air makes a cut apple turn brown.

items.stem: Why should a conclusion be based only on the results of the experiment?
items.answer: Otherwise the conclusion reflects opinion or expectation instead of evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: evidence. 1 mark: avoids bias.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – draw a conclusion; Q – analyse the results; R – test it with an experiment; S – form a hypothesis.
items.answer: S → R → Q → P
items.markingKey: (a) Order: form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results → draw a conclusion.

items.stem: Rohan thinks that plants grow better in sunlight. Describe a simple experiment to test this idea.
items.answer: Grow two similar pots of seedlings, one in sunlight and one in a dark cupboard, water both equally and compare after a week.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two set-ups differing in only one factor. 1 mark: what is observed or measured and compared.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – form a hypothesis; Q – test it with an experiment; R – analyse the results; S – ask a question; T – observe.
items.answer: T → S → P → Q → R
items.markingKey: (a) Order: observe → ask a question → form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A hypothesis must be testable.
Reason (R): Only a testable idea can be supported or rejected by evidence from an experiment.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which step comes immediately after forming a hypothesis?
items.answer: Testing it by an experiment
items.markingKey: (a) Testing it by an experiment.

items.stem: Ishita thinks that sugar dissolves faster in hot water. Describe a simple experiment to test this idea.
items.answer: Add one spoon of sugar to equal amounts of hot and cold water and time how long it takes to dissolve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two set-ups differing in only one factor. 1 mark: what is observed or measured and compared.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – test it with an experiment; Q – form a hypothesis; R – analyse the results; S – draw a conclusion.
items.answer: Q → P → R → S
items.markingKey: (a) Order: form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results → draw a conclusion.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "Looking for patterns in recorded data, often using tables and graphs."
items.answer: analysis of results
items.markingKey: (d) Analysis of results is looking for patterns in recorded data, often using tables and graphs.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – analyse the results; Q – ask a question; R – form a hypothesis; S – test it with an experiment; T – observe.
items.answer: T → Q → R → S → P
items.markingKey: (d) Order: observe → ask a question → form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Scientists share their findings with others.
Reason (R): Other scientists can repeat the experiment and check the results.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains why findings are shared.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A possible explanation or answer to a question that can be tested."
items.answer: a hypothesis
items.markingKey: (c) A hypothesis is a possible explanation or answer to a question that can be tested.

items.stem: A good hypothesis must be:
items.answer: testable
items.markingKey: (a) testable.

items.stem: What is meant by the dependent variable?
items.answer: The factor that is measured or observed to see the effect of the change
items.markingKey: 1 mark: The dependent variable – the factor that is measured or observed to see the effect of the change.

items.stem: In an experiment to find how the temperature of water affects the time taken by sugar to dissolve, what does Dev measure (dependent variable)?
items.answer: time taken to dissolve
items.markingKey: (c) The time taken to dissolve is the result that is measured.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): In a fair test only one factor is changed at a time.
Reason (R): If two factors are changed together, we cannot tell which one caused the result.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Priya measured the time for 20 oscillations of a pendulum three times and recorded 15.9 s, 14.6 s and 16.2 s. Find the average (mean) value and say why repeating is useful.
items.markingKey: (15.9 + 14.6 + 16.2) ÷ 3 = 46.7 ÷ 3 = 15.6 s (1 mark); repeating reduces the effect of errors and makes the result reliable (1 mark).

items.stem: Priya and Mehak tested how the amount of water given affects the height of bean plants. They changed the amount of water given each day, but they also changed the type of soil at the same time. Explain why their test is not fair and how to correct it.
items.answer: Two factors changed, so we cannot tell whether the amount of water given each day or the type of soil caused the change in the height of the plants. Keep the type of soil the same and change only the amount of water given each day.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two variables changed so effect cannot be linked to one. 1 mark: keep all except one factor the same.

items.stem: A class recorded the time taken for 5 g of sugar to dissolve in 100 mL of water at different temperatures: 20 °C – 184 s; 40 °C – 159 s; 60 °C – 132 s; 70 °C – 101 s. (i) Name the independent and dependent variables. (ii) What pattern do you see? (iii) Predict the time at a temperature higher than 70 °C.
items.answer: (i) Independent: water temperature; dependent: time to dissolve. (ii) The higher the temperature, the less time sugar takes to dissolve. (iii) Less than 101 s.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The factors that are kept the same so that the test is fair."
items.answer: controlled variables
items.markingKey: (c) Controlled variables is the factors that are kept the same so that the test is fair.

items.stem: Plan a fair test to find how the temperature of water affects the time taken by sugar to dissolve. Name the variable you will change, the variable you will measure and any two variables you will keep the same.
items.answer: Change: temperature of water. Measure: time taken to dissolve. Keep the same: amount of sugar and volume of water (also type of sugar).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: independent variable, dependent variable, two controlled variables.

items.stem: Diya measured the time for 20 oscillations of a pendulum three times and recorded 16.3 s, 16.4 s and 17.5 s. Find the average (mean) value and say why repeating is useful.
items.markingKey: (16.3 + 16.4 + 17.5) ÷ 3 = 50.2 ÷ 3 = 16.7 s (1 mark); repeating reduces the effect of errors and makes the result reliable (1 mark).

items.stem: For a fair test of how the amount of water given affects the height of bean plants, which of these must be kept the same?
items.answer: amount of sunlight
items.markingKey: (a) Amount of sunlight is a controlled variable; only the amount of water given each day is changed.
options: amount of water given each day

items.stem: Plan a fair test to find how the amount of salt affects the freezing time of water. Name the variable you will change, the variable you will measure and any two variables you will keep the same.
items.answer: Change: amount of salt added. Measure: time taken to freeze. Keep the same: volume of water and freezer used (also type of container).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: independent variable, dependent variable, two controlled variables.

items.stem: A class recorded the time taken for 5 g of sugar to dissolve in 100 mL of water at different temperatures: 20 °C – 159 s; 30 °C – 145 s; 60 °C – 125 s; 70 °C – 110 s. (i) Name the independent and dependent variables. (ii) What pattern do you see? (iii) Predict the time at a temperature higher than 70 °C.
items.answer: (i) Independent: water temperature; dependent: time to dissolve. (ii) The higher the temperature, the less time sugar takes to dissolve. (iii) Less than 110 s.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem:
Read: Pooja timed how long ice cubes took to melt on plates made of steel, plastic and wood, all kept in the same room. Steel: 18 min; plastic: 31 min; wood: 35 min.
(i) What was the independent variable? (ii) What was measured? (iii) Which material conducts heat best? Give a reason. (iv) Name two things she must keep the same.
items.answer: (i) Material of the plate. (ii) Time for the ice to melt. (iii) Steel, because ice melted fastest on it, so heat reached the ice fastest. (iv) Size of ice cube, room temperature, size/thickness of plate (any two).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each part.

items.stem: Plan a fair test to find how the surface affects the distance a marble rolls. Name the variable you will change, the variable you will measure and any two variables you will keep the same.
items.answer: Change: type of surface. Measure: distance rolled. Keep the same: the same marble and height of release (also slope of the ramp).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: independent variable, dependent variable, two controlled variables.

items.stem: Rahul measured the distance rolled by a toy car three times and recorded 85.0 cm, 101.8 cm and 85.0 cm. Find the average (mean) value and say why repeating is useful.
items.markingKey: (85.0 + 101.8 + 85.0) ÷ 3 = 271.8 ÷ 3 = 90.6 cm (1 mark); repeating reduces the effect of errors and makes the result reliable (1 mark).

items.stem:
Read: Kunal wanted to know whether fertiliser helps wheat seedlings grow. He took two pots. Pot A had garden soil and fertiliser and was kept in the sun. Pot B had sand without fertiliser and was kept indoors. After two weeks, Pot A seedlings were taller.
(i) Is this a fair test? (ii) Name two factors other than fertiliser that differed. (iii) Can Kunal conclude that fertiliser made the seedlings taller? (iv) How should he redo the test?
items.answer: (i) No. (ii) Type of soil (soil vs sand) and sunlight. (iii) No, because the height difference may be due to soil or sunlight. (iv) Use the same soil, pot size, water and sunlight for both pots; add fertiliser only to one.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each part.

items.stem: Science is best described as:
items.answer: a way of finding out about the world through questions, observation and evidence
items.markingKey: (b) Science is a process; ideas are tested and revised when new evidence appears.
options: a fixed list of facts that never changes
a way of finding out about the world through questions, observation and evidence
a collection of opinions of famous people
only the work done in big laboratories

items.stem: Priya and Arjun tested how the temperature of water affects the time taken by sugar to dissolve. They changed the temperature of water, but they also changed the volume of water at the same time. Explain why their test is not fair and how to correct it.
items.answer: Two factors changed, so we cannot tell whether the temperature of water or the volume of water caused the change in the time taken to dissolve. Keep the volume of water the same and change only the temperature of water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two variables changed so effect cannot be linked to one. 1 mark: keep all except one factor the same.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – analyse the results; Q – test it with an experiment; R – form a hypothesis; S – observe; T – ask a question; U – draw a conclusion.
items.answer: S → T → R → Q → P → U
items.markingKey: (c) Order: observe → ask a question → form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results → draw a conclusion.
options: Q → U → P → R → T → S
U → R → T → Q → S → P
S → T → R → Q → P → U
S → T → U → R → P → Q

items.stem: Harleen is investigating how the temperature of water affects the time taken by sugar to dissolve. Which is the variable that Harleen changes (independent variable)?
items.answer: temperature of water
items.markingKey: (a) The factor deliberately changed is the temperature of water; the time taken to dissolve is measured.

items.stem: Aarav thinks a dark coloured cloth heats up faster in sunlight. Describe a simple experiment to test this idea.
items.answer: Wrap two identical bottles of water in black and white cloth, keep them in the sun and measure the temperature after 30 minutes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two set-ups differing in only one factor. 1 mark: what is observed or measured and compared.

items.stem: Which of the following is a question that cannot be tested in an experiment?
items.answer: Which festival is the most enjoyable?
items.markingKey: (c) Which festival is the most enjoyable? is a question that cannot be tested in an experiment. The others: Does salt dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water? – a testable question; Does a ball bounce higher on a cement floor than on grass? – a testable question; Does a plant kept in the dark stay green? – a testable question.
options: Does a ball bounce higher on a cement floor than on grass?
Does a plant kept in the dark stay green?
Which festival is the most enjoyable?
Does salt dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water?

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The set-up kept without the change being tested, used for comparison."
items.answer: a control set-up
items.markingKey: (d) A control set-up is the set-up kept without the change being tested, used for comparison.

items.stem: Manish and Zoya tested how the colour of a container affects how fast the water in it warms in sunlight. They changed the colour of the container, but they also changed the size and material of container at the same time. Explain why their test is not fair and how to correct it.
items.answer: Two factors changed, so we cannot tell whether the colour of the container or the size and material of container caused the change in the rise in water temperature. Keep the size and material of container the same and change only the colour of the container.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two variables changed so effect cannot be linked to one. 1 mark: keep all except one factor the same.

items.stem: Ananya thinks that seeds need water to germinate. Which of these is the hypothesis being tested?
items.answer: Seeds need water to germinate.
items.markingKey: (a) The hypothesis is the testable idea: "Seeds need water to germinate."
options: Plants need sunlight to grow well.
Dark cloth absorbs more heat than white cloth.

items.stem: A class recorded the time taken for 5 g of sugar to dissolve in 100 mL of water at different temperatures: 20 °C – 200 s; 30 °C – 175 s; 40 °C – 155 s; 50 °C – 132 s. (i) Name the independent and dependent variables. (ii) What pattern do you see? (iii) Predict the time at a temperature higher than 50 °C.
items.answer: (i) Independent: water temperature; dependent: time to dissolve. (ii) The higher the temperature, the less time sugar takes to dissolve. (iii) Less than 132 s.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Sort these statements into an inference and an observation: (1) The plant has not been watered for days; (2) The iron nail has a brown coating; (3) The candle flame went out when covered with a glass; (4) The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat
items.answer: An inference: The plant has not been watered for days; The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat. An observation: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass; The iron nail has a brown coating.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): An inference: The plant has not been watered for days; The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat. An observation: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass; The iron nail has a brown coating.

items.stem: In an experiment to find how the amount of water given affects the height of bean plants, what does Aditi measure (dependent variable)?
items.answer: height of the plants
items.markingKey: (b) The height of the plants is the result that is measured.
options: amount of water given each day

items.stem: Plan a fair test to find how the amount of water given affects the height of bean plants. Name the variable you will change, the variable you will measure and any two variables you will keep the same.
items.answer: Change: amount of water given each day. Measure: height of the plants. Keep the same: type of plant and size of pot (also amount of sunlight).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: independent variable, dependent variable, two controlled variables.

items.stem: Kavya thinks that salt water freezes more slowly than plain water. Describe a simple experiment to test this idea.
items.answer: Keep equal cups of plain and salt water in the freezer and check them every 15 minutes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two set-ups differing in only one factor. 1 mark: what is observed or measured and compared.

items.stem: Which tool is most useful for spotting a pattern in measurements?
items.answer: A table or graph of the data
items.markingKey: (c) A table or graph of the data.
options: A table or graph of the data

items.stem: Which term is described here? "Observations and measurements that support or reject an idea."
items.answer: evidence
items.markingKey: (b) Evidence is observations and measurements that support or reject an idea.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is an observation?
items.answer: The milk has turned sour and smells bad.
items.markingKey: (a) The milk has turned sour and smells bad. is an observation. The others: The milk was left out too long and microbes spoiled it. – an inference; The flame needs air to keep burning. – an inference; The plant has not been watered for days. – an inference.
options: The milk has turned sour and smells bad.
The milk was left out too long and microbes spoiled it.
The flame needs air to keep burning.
The plant has not been watered for days.

items.stem: Why is a hypothesis not the same as a guess?
items.answer: A hypothesis is based on observations and can be tested by an experiment; a random guess need not be.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: based on observation/prior knowledge. 1 mark: testable.

items.stem: Nandini read online that eating carrots lets you see in total darkness. Explain how she could use science to judge this claim.
items.answer: Check the evidence and source; know that vitamin A in carrots prevents night blindness but cannot make eyes see without any light; a simple test in a dark room shows nobody can see with no light.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: question the source/evidence. 1 mark: correct science. 1 mark: test or reasoning.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – test it with an experiment; Q – draw a conclusion; R – analyse the results; S – form a hypothesis.
items.answer: S → P → R → Q
items.markingKey: (c) Order: form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results → draw a conclusion.

items.stem: Which of these is the best first step when you notice something puzzling in nature?
items.answer: Ask a clear question about it
items.markingKey: (c) Science begins with observing carefully and asking a clear question.
options: Ask a friend to guess the answer
Ask a clear question about it
Ignore it if the textbook does not mention it

items.stem: Nandini and Ishaan tested how the number of batteries affects the brightness of a bulb. They changed the number of cells, but they also changed the the switch used at the same time. Explain why their test is not fair and how to correct it.
items.answer: Two factors changed, so we cannot tell whether the number of cells or the the switch used caused the change in the brightness of the bulb. Keep the the switch used the same and change only the number of cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two variables changed so effect cannot be linked to one. 1 mark: keep all except one factor the same.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – ask a question; Q – form a hypothesis; R – analyse the results; S – test it with an experiment; T – observe.
items.answer: T → P → Q → S → R
items.markingKey: (d) Order: observe → ask a question → form a hypothesis → test it with an experiment → analyse the results.

items.stem: Diya is investigating how the number of batteries affects the brightness of a bulb. Which is the variable that Diya changes (independent variable)?
items.answer: number of cells
items.markingKey: (b) The factor deliberately changed is the number of cells; the brightness of the bulb is measured.

items.stem: Diya thinks that a cut apple turns brown faster in air. Describe a simple experiment to test this idea.
items.answer: Keep one cut piece in open air and one wrapped tightly in cling film; compare after an hour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two set-ups differing in only one factor. 1 mark: what is observed or measured and compared.

items.stem: Which of the following is a testable question?
items.answer: Does a ball bounce higher on a cement floor than on grass?
items.markingKey: (c) Does a ball bounce higher on a cement floor than on grass? is a testable question. The others: Is a rose nicer than a lotus? – a question that cannot be tested in an experiment; Which colour is the most beautiful? – a question that cannot be tested in an experiment; Which festival is the most enjoyable? – a question that cannot be tested in an experiment.
options: Is a rose nicer than a lotus?
Which festival is the most enjoyable?
Does a ball bounce higher on a cement floor than on grass?
Which colour is the most beautiful?

items.stem: Which term is described here? "An experiment in which only one factor is changed and all others are kept the same."
items.answer: a fair test
items.markingKey: (b) A fair test is an experiment in which only one factor is changed and all others are kept the same.

items.stem: Ananya and Zoya tested how the temperature of water affects the time taken by sugar to dissolve. They changed the temperature of water, but they also changed the amount of sugar at the same time. Explain why their test is not fair and how to correct it.
items.answer: Two factors changed, so we cannot tell whether the temperature of water or the amount of sugar caused the change in the time taken to dissolve. Keep the amount of sugar the same and change only the temperature of water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two variables changed so effect cannot be linked to one. 1 mark: keep all except one factor the same.

items.stem: Arjun thinks that a wet cloth dries faster in wind. Which of these is the hypothesis being tested?
items.answer: Wind speeds up drying.
items.markingKey: (a) The hypothesis is the testable idea: "Wind speeds up drying."
options: Balls bounce higher on hard surfaces.
Plants need sunlight to grow well.

items.stem: A class recorded the time taken for 5 g of sugar to dissolve in 100 mL of water at different temperatures: 10 °C – 169 s; 20 °C – 148 s; 40 °C – 122 s; 50 °C – 98 s. (i) Name the independent and dependent variables. (ii) What pattern do you see? (iii) Predict the time at a temperature higher than 50 °C.
items.answer: (i) Independent: water temperature; dependent: time to dissolve. (ii) The higher the temperature, the less time sugar takes to dissolve. (iii) Less than 98 s.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Sort these statements into an observation and an inference: (1) The flame needs air to keep burning; (2) The milk has turned sour and smells bad; (3) The candle flame went out when covered with a glass; (4) The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat
items.answer: An observation: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass; The milk has turned sour and smells bad. An inference: The flame needs air to keep burning; The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): An observation: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass; The milk has turned sour and smells bad. An inference: The flame needs air to keep burning; The water of the puddle evaporated in the heat.

items.stem: In an experiment to find how the amount of salt affects the freezing time of water, what does Farhan measure (dependent variable)?
items.answer: time taken to freeze
items.markingKey: (d) The time taken to freeze is the result that is measured.

items.stem: Plan a fair test to find how the length of a pendulum affects the time of one oscillation. Name the variable you will change, the variable you will measure and any two variables you will keep the same.
items.answer: Change: length of the thread. Measure: time for one oscillation. Keep the same: mass of the bob and angle of release (also type of thread).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: independent variable, dependent variable, two controlled variables.

items.stem: Ananya thinks that seeds need water to germinate. Describe a simple experiment to test this idea.
items.answer: Keep moong seeds on dry cotton and on wet cotton for three days and compare.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two set-ups differing in only one factor. 1 mark: what is observed or measured and compared.

items.stem: Why is it useful to share findings with others?
items.answer: Others can check, repeat and build on the work
items.markingKey: (c) Others can check, repeat and build on the work.
options: It avoids the need to record data
It guarantees the result is correct
Others can check, repeat and build on the work

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A statement of what we expect to happen in a test, based on our idea."
items.answer: a prediction
items.markingKey: (d) A prediction is a statement of what we expect to happen in a test, based on our idea.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is an observation?
items.answer: The candle flame went out when covered with a glass.
items.markingKey: (b) The candle flame went out when covered with a glass. is an observation. The others: The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air. – an inference; The milk was left out too long and microbes spoiled it. – an inference; The flame needs air to keep burning. – an inference.
options: The nail rusted because it was kept in moist air.
The candle flame went out when covered with a glass.
The milk was left out too long and microbes spoiled it.
The flame needs air to keep burning.

items.stem: Why do scientists keep a detailed record of how they did an experiment?
items.answer: So that others can repeat it exactly and check whether they get the same results.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: repeatability. 1 mark: checking.

items.stem: A TV advertisement claims, "Our toothpaste makes teeth 3 times stronger." What questions would a scientist ask before accepting this claim?
items.answer: Stronger compared with what? How was strength measured? How many people were tested, and was there a fair comparison with another toothpaste? Who did the test, and can it be repeated?
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for any three valid questions about evidence, comparison, measurement or repeatability.

items.stem: Arrange these steps of a scientific investigation in the correct order: P – analyse the results; Q – share the findings; R – draw a conclusion; S – test it with an experiment.
items.answer: S → P → R → Q
items.markingKey: (a) Order: test it with an experiment → analyse the results → draw a conclusion → share the findings.
